title: Productive staple farming with seawater and a closed salt balance

concept.text: Proposed innovation: a farming system that produces nutritionally significant staple food using seawater as its principal irrigation source while maintaining sustainable water and salt balances over time. The advance combines a productive salt-tolerant crop with agronomy, irrigation, drainage and environmental protection. A plant's ability to survive salty water would address only one part of the goal.

Conceptual clarification: a closed salt balance means accounting for incoming salt, its storage within the system and its eventual removal or containment. It does not mean assuming that salt disappears or that every material stream must circulate indefinitely. The system would need to explain where salt goes and how its management protects the productive growing environment, groundwater and neighboring ecosystems.

significance.text: Conditional significance: if staple crops could achieve useful yields and acceptable costs under these conditions, suitable coastal and arid locations could produce food with substantially less freshwater irrigation. The revolutionary capability would be the combination of food productivity, seawater use and durable environmental performance, rather than salt tolerance considered alone.

Conditional downstream possibilities include additional agricultural production and reduced competition for freshwater. Their scale would depend on suitable land, seawater conveyance, energy, drainage infrastructure, salt disposal or containment, economics and ecological constraints. Seawater use alone would not establish net freshwater savings: freshwater used for crop establishment, dilution, flushing or other operations would also need to be counted. The proposal therefore does not imply that all coastal land becomes farmland or that regional water scarcity would automatically be resolved.

missing_breakthrough.text: Target capability: integrate staple-food productivity at seawater-level salinity with a farm system that manages incoming salt for multiple growing seasons. The supplied evidence does not establish whether this complete capability remains absent from the field. It does, however, define a coherent target whose crop, engineering and environmental requirements must be demonstrated together.

Proposed engineering and scientific questions include whether a candidate crop can maintain harvestable yield and nutritional value throughout its life cycle under the intended irrigation conditions; how the growing environment remains productive as salt enters; and how drainage, salt removal or containment can operate at acceptable cost. Crop survival, a single successful harvest and sustainable staple production are different levels of accomplishment.

System-level synthesis: moving salt away from the crop would not by itself settle the environmental problem. A convincing design must identify the destination and consequences of salt-bearing drainage or other exported material, including effects beyond the farm boundary. These are requirements of the proposed system; the supplied retained scientific material does not independently establish their quantitative severity or the best technical solution.

current_state.text: The supplied research reports seawater-irrigated salt-tolerant crops and experimental plants, but the validated review could not verify those demonstrations from the retained material. No usable field-trial text, measured crop yields, seawater fractions, production costs or multi-year salt balances were supplied. Existing partial achievements and the availability of a competitive staple-food system therefore remain unresolved in this record. This evidence gap does not show that the reported demonstrations are false or that the proposed system is impossible.

The research identifies a paper attributed to Josefin Thorslund, Marc F. P. Bierkens and colleagues, titled “Common irrigation drivers of freshwater salinisation in river basins worldwide,” dated 9 July 2021, and describes findings from seven river basins. However, the validated review reports that the retained PubMed copy contains only a cookie-access message, with no abstract, results or bibliographic text confirming the paper's identity. Consequently, the date, seven-basin scope and reported irrigation-related findings are supplied research metadata, not verified scientific findings in this record. The earlier description of an abstract-only assessment must be corrected to an access-limited assessment with no scientific text available.

The research also reports finding a potentially relevant seawater-irrigated halophyte field-trial paper whose publisher page returned an access error. The review received neither retained field-trial text nor a record documenting that access attempt. Its methods and results cannot therefore be used to establish an achievement here. Even if the reported river-basin study were verified, evidence about irrigation-related freshwater salinisation would inform a management constraint; it would not by itself establish the feasibility or impossibility of seawater staple farming.

No bounded freshness search record was supplied to establish the field's status as of 1 November 2026. The source index records a retrieval on 11 November 2026, but a retrieval date does not establish the recency or completeness of scientific coverage. The supplied materials consequently support neither a claim that the full innovation has been achieved nor a definitive claim that it remains unachieved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate a farm-scale system for several years that produces a nutritionally significant staple crop using predominantly seawater, with yields and costs competitive against explicitly identified local alternatives. Before testing, define the seawater share, irrigation salinity, production area, duration, nutritional contribution and economic comparison. These are proposed evaluation criteria, not established consensus thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Multiyear seawater staple farming achieves competitive yields and costs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed accounting and environmental demonstration: publish complete water and salt balances covering inputs, outputs and changes in storage. Include freshwater used at every production stage, salt retained in the growing environment, salt exported in harvested material or drainage, and the destination of managed waste streams. Show that productive growing conditions persist and that groundwater and neighboring ecosystems meet predefined, site-appropriate protection criteria. Explain measurement uncertainty and any material balance that remains unclosed.
completion_criteria.label: Complete water and salt balances demonstrate sustained, environmentally protected production

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: make methods, measurements and cost assumptions available for independent assessment and replication. Test enough seasons and locations to characterize performance under the conditions claimed, and report failures and operating limits alongside successful trials. Results should specify crop, climate, soil or growing medium, seawater composition, infrastructure and energy requirements. Finite trials would establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions, not literal universality across staple crops or farming environments.
completion_criteria.label: Available methods and multiseason, multisite results document practical operating limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: AGR-01, “Cereal crops supplied predominantly by biological nitrogen fixation,” and AGR-02, “A transferable carbon-concentrating system for C3 staple crops,” address different crop capabilities that could potentially complement seawater farming. Biological nitrogen supply concerns crop nutrition; carbon concentration concerns photosynthetic performance. Neither title implies seawater tolerance or a sustainable farm salt balance.

Roster-based synthesis: AGR-03, “Reliable clonal seed reproduction across major hybrid crops,” concerns reproduction and the preservation of hybrid combinations. AGR-04, “High-yield perennial versions of the major grain-crop portfolio,” concerns productive perennial growth. Either capability might be combined with a suitable seawater crop, but neither establishes productivity under seawater irrigation or resolves salt management over time.

Roster-based synthesis: AGR-06, “Rapidly programmable, durable crop immunity,” addresses disease resistance, while AGR-07, “A general, rapid method for creating productive crops from wild plants,” could offer a route for developing productive crops from salt-tolerant wild candidates. That possible connection does not make the concepts equivalent: seawater staple farming could use several crop-development approaches, and any candidate would still require agronomic, nutritional, economic and salt-balance validation.

Roster-based synthesis: AGR-08, “Economically accessible, end-to-end autonomous field farming,” could overlap through automated irrigation, monitoring and drainage operations, but autonomy does not establish seawater compatibility or environmental performance. AGR-09, “Food crops that reliably build durable, additional soil carbon,” shares an interest in long-term growing conditions and environmental outcomes, but durable additional carbon storage and sustainable salt management are separate achievements requiring separate evidence.

unresolved_issues: The retained PubMed artifact does not verify the claimed paper's identity, publication date, seven-basin scope or scientific findings.
The crop demonstrations and potentially relevant halophyte field trial lack supplied scientific text sufficient to assess species, salinity, yield, nutrition, duration, economics or salt management.
The reported publisher access failure has no supplied retained artifact or search record documenting it.
The absence of a bounded freshness search leaves the availability of a complete system unresolved as of 1 November 2026; the later retrieval timestamp does not resolve this.
Operational definitions remain to be set for predominantly seawater, farm scale, nutritionally significant production, competitive yield and cost, and acceptable environmental performance.
No supplied measurements establish net freshwater savings, long-term salt storage, drainage impacts or the cost and environmental consequences of salt removal or containment.

brief.title: Staple food grown with seawater and salt kept in check
possible: Farmers in suitable coastal and dry regions could grow staple food using mainly seawater. The farm would account for where incoming salt accumulates and how it is removed or contained, keeping the growing environment productive over time.
why: This could expand food production while reducing competition for freshwater. Farmers would gain another irrigation source, and surrounding communities could face less demand on freshwater supplies.

sources.who: Josefin Thorslund, Marc F. P. Bierkens and colleagues
sources.showed: They found that irrigation withdrawals, water returning from farms and irrigated area were associated with higher or increasing salt levels in rivers.
sources.cited_for: Irrigation can contribute to salt problems beyond the farm.
sources.not_established: The study does not test seawater farming or establish how a staple-food farm could manage its salt.

sources.who: E. P. Glenn, J. W. O'Leary, M. C. Watson, T. L. Thompson and R. O. Kuehl
sources.showed: They grew Salicornia bigelovii, a salt-tolerant plant with oil-rich seeds, using seawater over six years. Seed and plant yields matched or exceeded freshwater oilseed crops.
sources.quote: Yields of seed and biomass equaled or exceeded freshwater oilseed crops such as soybean and sunflower.
sources.cited_for: A salt-tolerant oilseed crop can produce substantial harvests under direct seawater irrigation.
sources.not_established: The trials do not establish competitive total costs, staple nutritional adequacy or lasting environmental protection.

sources.who: Mansoor Al-Tamimi, Steve Green and colleagues
sources.showed: A single-season trial compared salty irrigation waters and delivery systems for Salicornia. Fish-farm wastewater improved production, while drainage carried salt toward groundwater. Revenue came mainly from fresh edible tips.
sources.quote: The value derives primarily from fresh tips.
sources.cited_for: Irrigation choices affect both crop production and the salt carried below the growing area.
sources.not_established: Revenue from fresh tips does not establish competitive staple-food costs or safe long-term salt disposal.

sources.who: Mansoor Al-Tamimi, Steve Green and colleagues
sources.showed: In a follow-up trial, salt and nitrogen applied in irrigation drained back into underground water stores. A model predicted rising salt concentrations there.
sources.quote: Field measurements of drainage and leaching under the crop showed that all of the salt and nitrogen from the groundwater was returned back to the aquifer as leachate.
sources.cited_for: Keeping salt out of the crop's growing area can transfer the problem into groundwater.
sources.not_established: Returning salt underground does not demonstrate environmentally protected production over many seasons.

sources.who: Oscar Bianciotto, Fernando Aras Martin and colleagues
sources.showed: A small pot trial in Tierra del Fuego tested seawater delivered through drippers to Salicornia magellanica. Older plants produced the highest yields in the third season.
sources.quote:
The irrigation 
flow showed different effects on the production parameters 
and plant age, with highest yields recorded in more develo -
ped plants at the third season.
sources.cited_for: Seawater crop performance depends on plant maturity and growing conditions.
sources.not_established: Small pot trials do not establish farm-scale staple yields, competitive costs or a complete salt balance.

shown: Glenn and colleagues demonstrated sustained seawater irrigation of an oilseed crop, with harvests comparable to conventional oilseed crops. This goes beyond merely keeping plants alive in salty water.
Al-Tamimi and colleagues measured salt draining beneath Salicornia crops. Their work exposes the central challenge: moving salt away from roots can leave groundwater with an increasing salt burden.
missing: A complete demonstration would need useful staple nutrition and competitive yields and costs over multiple years.
Water accounting would need to include freshwater used for establishment, dilution and flushing to establish net savings.
Salt accounting would need to show lasting protection of the growing environment, groundwater and neighboring ecosystems.
Independent trials would need to establish where the system works and where it fails.

milestones.label: A seawater staple farm delivers competitive harvests and costs
milestones.explanation: A farm-scale trial would have to produce nutritionally significant staple food mainly with seawater over several years, matching defined local alternatives on yield and cost. This would establish practical food production.

milestones.label: Water and salt accounting shows lasting environmental protection
milestones.explanation: Measurements would have to track all water and salt entering, leaving or accumulating, including waste destinations, while showing sustained production and environmental protection. This would establish that salt is managed safely.

milestones.label: Repeatable results establish where the system works
milestones.explanation: Trials across seasons and sites would have to share methods, measurements and cost assumptions, reporting failures and operating limits. This would establish the conditions under which others could reproduce the results.

uncertain: What seawater share, nutritional contribution and local cost comparison should qualify a farm as successful?
Can salt removal or containment protect surrounding environments at an acceptable cost?
Can Salicornia seed meal provide suitable staple nutrition despite its reported growth-inhibiting compounds?

page.title: Seawater-irrigated staple crops with salt balance
page.definition: A farming system produces grain or edible oil using direct seawater irrigation over repeated growing seasons. Salt balance means that incoming salt is accounted for through storage and removal, while crop production continues and groundwater and receiving ecosystems meet applicable environmental requirements.

goal.need: Agriculture accounts for 72% of global freshwater withdrawals in 2023. A study covering 401 river sub-basins in seven basins, using observations from 1980–2010, found increasing salinisation trends in 57% of sub-basins. These quantities motivate investigation of seawater irrigation together with control of salt accumulation and drainage.

statements.body: FAO-hosted Global Framework on Water Scarcity in Agriculture, Saline Agriculture Working Group
statements.quote: It is therefore important to support innovative and sustainable food production systems in increasingly saline soil and water environments.
Investigate the uptake of salt and other nutrients by Salicornia to reduce disposal to the environment
statements.context: An objective of its integrated agriculture–aquaculture experiment using reverse-osmosis brine and aquaculture effluent at 23,000 ppm, with three experimental replications.

completion.title: Independent field demonstrations reproduce seawater-grown staple production with farm-wide salt control.
completion.criterion: Independently repeated field operation produces grain or edible oil for human consumption over successive growing seasons using direct seawater irrigation. Sales cover production and salt-management costs. Measured water accounts include establishment, dilution and flushing, and establish freshwater savings against an identified local production system. Salt inputs, exports and changes in storage balance within measurement uncertainty, productive root-zone conditions persist, and groundwater and drainage meet applicable site-specific environmental requirements.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas synthesis of FAO saline-agriculture objectives and irrigation-management principles.
completion.basis: Searches of FAO guidance, ICBA programmes, seawater-agriculture standards, roadmaps and prize criteria found no combined completion test for staple production, economics and environmental salt control. This synthesis combines the published food-production objective with FAO's salt-balance and economic considerations. No universal minimum yield, freshwater saving, acreage or operating duration was found.

milestones.title: A candidate grain or oilseed crop reaches seed harvest under direct seawater irrigation.
milestones.criterion: A candidate crop produces harvestable seed in an experimental growing system irrigated directly with seawater. Epstein and Norlyn reported on 15 July 1977 that barley selections and cultivars grown in dune sand with Pacific Ocean water produced grain of feed quality, with rough yields approaching half the national barley average. Human-food suitability requires additional evidence.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas. Searches found experimental seed-production demonstrations but no published institutional pass criterion for this stage.

milestones.title: A seawater-irrigated grain or oilseed crop produces repeated field harvests.
milestones.criterion: Direct seawater irrigation supports seed harvests across successive field seasons, with yield and seed composition measured. Glenn and colleagues reported six years of Salicornia bigelovii field trials on 1 March 1991. Seed and biomass yields matched or exceeded soybean and sunflower benchmarks. Seeds contained 26–33% oil and 31% protein. Chicken-feeding experiments identified growth-inhibiting factors in the meal, attributed to saponins.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas. Searches found multiyear comparative field experiments but no externally prescribed minimum duration or staple-food yield.

milestones.title: Salt removal from an irrigated crop's root zone keeps pace with salt inputs.
milestones.criterion: At the maximum soil salinity compatible with the crop, removal must equal or exceed additional irrigation salt inputs. A related saline-water experiment in 2022–2023 used nine 8 × 8 m Salicornia plots and four drainage fluxmeters per plot. Mean salt input was 55.9 ± 26.9 kg/m² and measured leaching was 64.9 ± 37.9 kg/m², both mean ± SD. The authors interpreted these as balanced within variability and inferred salt return to groundwater.
milestones.set_by: FAO, The use of saline waters for crop production, Chapter 6. The principle applies generally to saline irrigation.
milestones.threshold_quote: at least as much salt as is brought in with additional irrigations must be removed from the rootzone

milestones.title: An integrated seawater farm sustains staple harvests, covers costs and controls exported salt.
milestones.criterion: One field system produces human-food grain or edible oil over successive seasons, covers production and salt-management costs, and maintains crop-compatible soil conditions. Its measured water account establishes freshwater savings against an identified local production system. Its farm-wide salt account reconciles inputs, storage and exports within measurement uncertainty, and groundwater and drainage meet applicable environmental requirements. This integrated operating result precedes independent repetition.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas. Searches of FAO guidance and ICBA programmes found component objectives and pilot experiments but no combined pre-completion acceptance test.

not_found: No external body was found prescribing a combined completion test for seawater-irrigated staple production, production economics and farm-wide environmental salt control.
No universal numerical thresholds were found for staple-food contribution, minimum yield, freshwater savings, farm area or demonstration duration.
No independently repeated demonstration satisfying the combined completion criterion was identified.
The opened abstracts of the 1977 barley and 1991 Salicornia studies do not provide experimental sample sizes.
The supplied Massey University drainage-study PDF and an ICBA-hosted copy both timed out.
The National Academies report pages opened without readable chapter text, and alternative chapter-text requests failed.

results.finding: Salicornia bigelovii produced seed during 6 years of direct-seawater field trials.
results.detail: The source reports oilseed production but does not establish human-food suitability.
results.quote: The terrestrial halophyte, Salicornia bigelovii Torr., was evaluated as an oilseed crop for direct seawater irrigation during 6 years of field trials in an extreme coastal desert environment. Yields of seed and biomass equaled or exceeded freshwater oilseed crops such as soybean and sunflower.

results.finding: Salicornia bigelovii produced seed in 6 years of direct-seawater field trials.
results.detail: Seed contained 26–33% oil and 31% protein. The meal contained growth-inhibiting factors attributed to saponins.
results.quote: The terrestrial halophyte, Salicornia bigelovii Torr., was evaluated as an oilseed crop for direct seawater irrigation during 6 years of field trials in an extreme coastal desert environment. Yields of seed and biomass equaled or exceeded freshwater oilseed crops such as soybean and sunflower.

results.finding: Salicornia bigelovii seed yield was 162.8 g/m² with aquabrine and drippers (n=5).
results.detail: Seed was harvested after irrigation with aquabrine, reverse-osmosis brine or saline groundwater, rather than direct seawater.

results.finding: Across nine Salicornia plots, mean salt input was 80 kg/m² and estimated leaching was 70 kg/m².
results.detail: The authors judged the balance reasonable given variability. Salt loss used measured leachate conductivity and modelled drainage; the study did not establish removal at the crop's maximum compatible soil salinity. Irrigation used saline waters rather than seawater.
results.quote:
The average amount of salt added across all nine

leaching in the upper part of the rootzone was on average 70 kg m� 2.

results.finding: Across nine Salicornia plots, mean salt leaching was 64.9 ± 37.9 kg/m².
results.detail: Mean salt input was 55.9 ± 26.9 kg/m²; the authors considered input and leaching balanced within variability. The plots used saline groundwater and brines, not direct seawater, and the maximum crop-compatible soil salinity was not established.
